en: Unopened, in its sealed liquid, to the printed date at 0–5 °C. The liquid is the storage medium, not packing waste: it is lightly salted whey or brine that keeps the curd hydrated and holds a salt concentration at the surface where contamination would otherwise land. Never pour it away until you are ready to eat.

Once opened, keep the ball fully submerged in its own liquid in a sealed tub — top it up with lightly salted water if you have lost some — and eat within about a week. Cloudy, ropy or sour-smelling liquid means it goes. Do not store it in plain water: that leaches salt out of the curd and leaves you with a sweeter, wetter, less protected cheese.
Only for cooking. Drain it, blot it, freeze it in a block, and use it grated on a pizza. Thawed fresh mozzarella weeps and turns squeaky.

Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture lists mulberry among fruit that must be refrigerated. Do not wash before storing, and keep in a shallow single layer so the weight of the fruit does not crush the bottom layer.
Freeze in a single layer on a tray first, then bag, so the berries do not clump.

Taiwan's 農業部 states plainly that finished mullet roe must be kept frozen or refrigerated — the salting takes only about 10–15 % of the roe weight and three to five days of sun-drying, which is not enough to make it shelf-stable. Keep it vacuum-packed or tightly wrapped at 4 °C or below and cut only what you will grill.

農業部 notes that stored too long — beyond about four months — the fat oxidises and the roe turns from amber to dull dark red. That colour change is the practical end of its life, before anything unsafe happens.
Keep the beans in an airtight container as it’s imperative that they remain dry.
Never refrigerate wet sprouts. Transfer to a plastic bag or use a glass or plastic container.

Refrigeration ensures that commercial sauces and condiments stay fresh for a longer period of time. Shelf-stable commercial mustard is safe when stored at room temperature after opening. Quality, not safety, is the reason the labels on these products suggest that they be refrigerated after opening.

Naan holds better than chapati because it is leavened and enriched with yoghurt, milk or ghee, but it is still a moist bread — sealed in a bag at room temperature it moulds rather than dries. Packaged supermarket naan carries preservatives and a printed date; go by that instead.
Refrigeration is the anti-mould move, not a freshness move. Reheat under a grill or on a tawa with a flick of water to steam it back.
The best option by a distance. Freeze flat with paper between, and reheat from frozen.
Freezing not recommended - may negatively impact the texture.

A true yam is a keeping crop: cool, dark, dry and above all well ventilated, spread out rather than piled, and never in a plastic bag. Check for soft spots and sprouting, and rub sprouts off as they appear. Seal a cut face and use that tuber within days.

Do not refrigerate a whole ñame. Like other tropical roots it is chilling sensitive, and a cold fridge brings internal browning and rot on faster than a cool pantry does. Refrigerate only peeled or cut pieces, submerged in water, for a day or two.
Peel, cube and boil, then freeze; or freeze the cooked, pounded purée. Raw frozen yam turns grey and watery.

Nameko is naturally coated in a gel, so the usual slimy-means-spoiled test does not apply — judge it by smell and by whether the caps have gone brown and mushy. Keep the sealed pack cold and use it soon; it spoils faster than any other cultivated mushroom.
Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture: wrap the head in a large sheet of paper and stand it at an angle in a cool place — it stays fresh several days that way, though the fridge is better.
Ohio State gives cabbage 1 to 2 weeks in a crisper or moisture-resistant wrap. Keep the head whole; peel leaves off as you need them rather than cutting it in half.

Use the printed 賞味期限. Japan's natto-industry HACCP guide, published via MHLW, requires the chiller to run at 10 °C or below and explains why: after fermentation the packs are chilled specifically to stop Bacillus subtilis var. natto fermenting further. Held warm or held too long the culture keeps working — the smell turns to ammonia and white tyrosine crystals appear on the beans. That is over-fermentation rather than acute spoilage, but it is the point to stop eating it.
Freeze in the unopened pack; thaw overnight in the fridge, not on the counter. Freezing halts the culture, which is exactly what you want.

USDA Agriculture Handbook 66: whole pads hold good quality for 3 weeks at 5 °C (41 °F) or 2 weeks at 10 °C (50 °F) at 95–99 % humidity. They are chilling sensitive below 10 °C, so past three weeks in a cold fridge expect bronzing and decay at the cut stem end. Scrape or singe off every spine and glochid first, keep them dry, and do not sprinkle or top-ice them.
Blanch or griddle the diced pads first to purge the viscous sap, drain well, then freeze.

Japan's MAFF: keep dried goods away from heat, sunlight and damp and close the pack tightly. Nori goes limp faster than any other dried seaweed — keep the desiccant sachet in the bag and reseal after every use. A limp sheet crisps up again over a low flame.
Unopened packs freeze well and this is the standard way to keep a bulk purchase. Let the pack come back to room temperature before opening it, or condensation will ruin the sheets.

Sealed, cool, dark and dry, to its printed date. Nougat is a supersaturated sugar and honey syrup aerated with egg white and loaded with nuts — the sugar binds the water and there is very little left for anything to grow in. Its enemy is humidity, not bacteria: nougat is strongly hygroscopic and a bar left open in a damp kitchen goes sticky, then weeps syrup, then sets into a solid slab.

Re-wrap it airtight the moment you open it, edible rice paper and all — the paper is there to stop it sticking, not to protect it. Keep it away from steam and from the hob. The nuts are the other clock: almonds, pistachios and hazelnuts eventually go rancid, and that shows up as a bitter, crayon-like aftertaste.
Avoid it. A fridge is humid, and taking cold nougat out into a warm room condenses water straight onto the surface — which is the exact thing that ruins it. Cool and dry beats cold and damp.
Highly perishable when stored in the pantry.

Treat onigiri as same-day food and keep it cool. MAFF’s bento guidance is to shape rice with cling film or disposable gloves rather than bare hands (Staphylococcus aureus lives on skin and its toxin is heat-stable), to let the rice cool completely before packing so steam does not condense inside, and to carry the box with an ice pack in warm weather.

MHLW’s hygiene guide for school-meal rice says cooked rice must not be carried over past the day it was cooked, and that rice held after cooking goes above 55 °C or below 8 °C, for as short a time as possible. Refrigeration makes the rice hard; wrap tightly and let it come back to room temperature, or microwave it.
After prepared for drinking, good for up to 1 week.
Good for 1 week after date on package.
Gut it the day you buy it and hold it at 4C or below; histamine-producing bacteria sit in the gills and guts.
An oily fish, so the freezer limit is quality rather than safety - the fat turns rancid before anything else goes wrong.

Cooked rice is the governing ingredient, and the FSA's rule for it is blunt: chill leftover rice 'as quickly as possible, ideally within one hour', then 'keep rice in the fridge for no more than one day until reheating'. A paellera holds an enormous amount of heat — get the rice off the pan and spread thin in shallow trays to cool, do not put the pan itself in the fridge. Reheat once only, until steaming hot all the way through, and never reheat it twice.

Freeze it in single portions the same evening, once cooled fast. Seafood paella suffers most — prawns and mussels turn rubbery — so pick the shellfish out and freeze the rice. Reheat from frozen with a splash of stock, covered, until steaming.

A dark cupboard away from the cooker, tightly capped. Palm oil is mostly saturated, which makes it one of the more stable cooking fats — but the failure mode is still rancidity, not bacteria: heat, light and air oxidise it, and rancid oil smells of old crayons or putty and tastes bitter. Unrefined red palm oil also fades from deep orange to pale yellow as its carotenes break down, which is a fair visual clock. It sets solid below about 24 °C and melts again with no harm done.
Decant a working amount into a small bottle and keep the bulk container closed — every opening brings in fresh air. Never pour used frying oil back into the jar.

Refrigeration slows oxidation but sets palm oil rock hard and makes it awkward to use, the same objection FoodKeeper raises against refrigerating coconut oil. Reach for it only if you have bought a large tin you will not finish for a year.

Wrap the bundle loosely in kitchen paper inside a bag in the crisper. The leaves are tough and waxy so they keep better than a soft herb, but they yellow from the cut ends and lose their vanilla-rice aroma as they go. Wash and dry them only when you are about to use them.

Freezing is the sensible option outside the tropics: rinse, dry, cut into lengths, bag flat. Frozen leaves are limp on thawing but the aroma survives well, and they can go straight into a pot of rice or a coconut syrup from frozen.

Keep it at or below 4 °C (40 °F). Paneer is a high-moisture, low-acid fresh cheese, which is exactly the profile the FDA describes for queso fresco-type cheeses as a favourable environment for Listeria — and Listeria grows in a cold fridge. Anything left in the 4–60 °C danger zone for more than two hours should go. Submerging the block in fresh water and changing the water daily keeps it soft, but it does not buy extra days.

No credible timeline exists for frozen paneer. It freezes without a safety problem but the curd tightens and turns rubbery and squeaky on thawing; cube it first, and use it in a simmered curry rather than fried fresh.

Sugar does not spoil. Keep the cone or block sealed in a bag or an airtight tin somewhere cool and dry; the enemies are humidity, which makes it sticky and eventually weeps molasses, and ants, which find it unerringly. A hardened, rock-solid block is still perfectly good — grate it, smash it in a bag, or dissolve it in hot water. Do not refrigerate it; the fridge is damp.

Sealed in its cellophane bag, somewhere cool and dark, to the printed date — and those dates really do run into months. This is not preservatives: a proper panettone is leavened with a stiff sourdough, carries a great deal of butter, egg yolk and sugar, and is baked to a low residual moisture. The sugar and fat bind and displace the water that mould and bacteria would otherwise need, and the acidity of the levain does the rest. Once you open the bag, the clock changes completely.

Opened, it dries out fast because of the very open, shredded crumb. Press the cut face against the bag, fold it closed, and eat it within the week. Stale panettone is the point of French toast and of the Milanese habit of dunking it — it is not a failure state.
Don't. Refrigeration accelerates staling and this is a bread, whatever the tin says. If your kitchen is warm and humid the freezer is the answer, not the fridge.
Freezes well whole in its bag, or in wedges. Thaw at room temperature and warm briefly.

The whole preservation system here is dryness. Keep the discs in a sealed jar or their original sealed sleeve, in a cool dark cupboard away from the stove. A papad that has gone soft and bendy has picked up moisture; sun it or give it a minute in a low oven before frying, and throw out anything showing mould or a musty smell. Cooked papads keep only hours before going limp.

Keep it frozen hard at −18 °C and cook straight from frozen — do not thaw. A pack that has softened and refrozen will have fused into one block and the layers will not separate on the griddle; that is a quality loss, but repeated thaw–refreeze on a dough carrying raw filling is also a safety question, so buy from a freezer that is genuinely cold.
Cooked parathas, cooled and wrapped.
Very delicate. Keep them dry and loosely bagged; any water trapped on the leaves turns them to slime overnight. Rooted punnets last longer than cut shoots.
Or package use-by date, whichever comes first.

Stand the stems in a small jar with a centimetre of water, bag the leaves loosely over the top and refrigerate; change the water every couple of days. Leaves stored flat in a sealed bag go black at the edges within days.
Ripen at room temperature first. Astringent varieties such as hachiya are only edible once fully soft; non-astringent ones such as fuyu can be eaten firm.
Refrigerate only after ripening. Commercial cold storage at −1 °C holds persimmons for 3 to 4 months, which a home refrigerator cannot reproduce.
Freeze the pulp rather than whole fruit. Freezing also removes astringency from hachiya-type fruit.
Only for a firm, well-dried cake in a cool dry room. The white bloom on the surface is crystallised sugar, not mould.

NCHFP gives dried fruit about 1 year at 60 °F and 6 months at 80 °F, and Ohio State advises refrigerating dried fruit where possible. Soft, semi-dried persimmon cakes are moist enough that the fridge is the right default.
Wrap individually; they thaw in minutes.

Refrigerate once opened, ginger kept under its liquid, lid on, 4 °C or below. Gari is a vinegar-and-sugar pickle so acidity is doing the work; NCHFP's rule is that the level of acidity in a pickled product is as important to its safety as it is to taste, and that pickling recipes assume vinegar at 5 percent acidity. Homemade gari made with a weak rice vinegar is not a preserve — keep it cold and eat it within a couple of weeks. Beni shoga in its plum brine is saltier and keeps better than sweet gari.
Unopened shelf-stable jars keep about a year in a cool dark cupboard; refrigerated packs from the chiller cabinet do not belong here at all.

An unopened commercial glass jar in wine or vinegar sauce, kept at or below 4 °C — never at room temperature, whatever the shelf you bought it from looked like. Home-marinated or deli-counter herring is a different thing altogether: it is a lightly salted raw fish sitting in a mild acid, it is not preserved to any meaningful degree, and it should be treated as a few days' food.

Once the jar is open, keep every fillet submerged in its brine or sauce at or below 4 °C and use a clean fork. Cold-marinated fish is a ready-to-eat food with a long chilled shelf life, which is precisely the category the FDA and Health Canada flag for Listeria — it grows at refrigerator temperature and the longer the food sits, the more of it there is.

Read this before you pickle your own. Salt and acid do not kill parasites; freezing does. The FDA's parasite-destruction conditions are −4 °F (−20 °C) or below for 7 days total, or −31 °F (−35 °C) until solid then held at −35 °C for 15 hours, or −35 °C until solid then held at −20 °C for 24 hours — and it notes these may not suit fish thicker than 6 inches. The FDA states in terms that 'brining and pickling may reduce the parasite hazard in a fish, but they do not eliminate it', and that nematode larvae have survived 28 days in a 21 %-salt brine. So the freezing is a treatment applied to the raw fish before marinating, not a way of storing the finished jar — pickled herring frozen after the fact goes mushy and cloudy.
Wrap and keep at 4C or below. This is cooked blood and cooked glutinous rice together - two of the most perishable things in a Taiwanese kitchen in one block.
Freezes well in portions; steam from frozen rather than thawing on the counter.
Store in a plastic bag within an airtight container.
Refrigeration of this item provides no benefit.
Freezing of this item provides no benefit.
Very soft skinned; CTAHR packs it no more than two layers deep in vented clamshells.
CTAHR: putting the clamshells into a cooler in the field can lengthen shelf life by as much as 10 days, depending on how ripe the fruit was when picked.
Freeze whole for juice and sorbet.

Sealed jar, cool dark cupboard. Like other dried starch flours it is stable while dry and finished once it is not — clumping, a musty smell, or any visible mould means the bag drew moisture. It darkens with age, which is oxidation of the fruit's own phenolics and a quality change rather than a safety one.

Unopened jars and bottles keep to the printed date in a cool dark cupboard. Plum sauce is a sugar-and-vinegar preserve — sweet, acidic and thick, which is exactly the combination that makes jam shelf-stable.

Refrigerate after opening. Any darkening at the neck of the jar is oxidation. Fuzzy mould on the surface of a sugary sauce means the whole jar goes — mould in a high-sugar food can be growing deeper than it looks.

New Mexico State University gives fresh chile 2 to 3 weeks at 45–50 °F (7–10 °C) and 90–95 % relative humidity. That is warmer than a domestic fridge: below that range the pods take chilling injury — softening, pitting and faster decay — so use the least cold drawer and expect the shorter end of the range.

Poblanos are almost always roasted and peeled first. NMSU: refrigerate or freeze roasted, peeled chile within 2 hours of roasting, press the air out of the bag, and it keeps safely in the freezer for up to 12 months. Roasted chile that stays in the fridge instead must be used or frozen within 3 days.

Airtight jar, cool dark cupboard, away from the hob. Poha is rolled flat, so far more surface is exposed to air than in a whole grain and it goes stale and faintly cardboardy long before rice would. It is also a favourite of pantry moths and weevils — check for webbing before you soak a batch. Thick poha survives storage better than the paper-thin kind.

Unopened, cool and dark. It is a strongly acidic sugar syrup, which is a hostile environment for microbes; what changes with age is the colour, which darkens towards black, and the flavour, which loses its fruitiness.
Cap it tightly and wipe the neck — a sticky thread down the outside of the bottle attracts mould and ants. Crystals or a thicker pour are normal and not spoilage.

Home-boiled pomegranate syrup, which is far less concentrated than the commercial article. USU gives one to two weeks refrigerated, or the freezer, for a home-made pomegranate syrup — treat that as the limit unless you reduced it to a true molasses.
A whole pomelo keeps well in a cool, ventilated spot. In Taiwan the fruit is traditionally left a few days after harvest to let the flesh sweeten.
Whole fruit only. Once segmented, keep the flesh in a sealed container and eat within a few days.
Unopened bottles keep to the printed date in a cool dark cupboard.

Refrigerate once opened. Ponzu is soy sauce cut with citrus juice and dashi, so it is both more dilute and more delicate than plain soy sauce — the citrus aroma is the first casualty of a bottle left on the counter. Homemade ponzu, which is fresh-squeezed juice with no pasteurisation, should be treated as a fresh food: keep it cold and use it within a week or two.
After opening time applies to prepared product.

Sealed commercial pork floss is shelf-stable because it is dried and often fried; heat and light turn the fat rancid, so keep the jar cool and dark rather than beside the stove. Always use a dry spoon — one damp spoonful will mould the whole jar.
After opening, an airtight container in the fridge keeps the fat from going rancid and keeps humidity out. If it clumps, darkens or smells like old oil, throw it out.

貢丸 are pre-cooked emulsified pork — a perishable cooked meat, not a cured sausage. Keep at 4 °C or below in a sealed box and reheat thoroughly. The springy texture comes from pounding and phosphates, not from any preservation step.
Freeze in portions; the emulsion goes crumbly after a couple of months and the fat picks up freezer taint.
From date of manufacturer.
This is the recommended storage method for whole potatoes.
The United States Potato Board notes refrigeration can cause potatoes to darken during cooking and to develop an unpleasantly sweet taste.
Freezer timeline applies to cooked and mashed potatoes.
3 - 5 year timetable based on cool temperatures, dark storage. May spoil as quickly as 3 months in hot temperatures.

Keep the fruit pushed under the brine — a lemon standing proud of the liquid is where mould starts — and skim any surface scum whenever you open the jar. Use a clean dry fork, never fingers. The brine goes syrupy and the peel goes translucent and soft over the first month; that is the cure working, not spoilage. Never cut back the salt in the recipe.

A cupboard jar is the traditional Moroccan practice and it is how most recipes are written, but it is not a practice any food-safety authority endorses for the home, and no defensible number can be given for it. The cure needs three to four weeks at room temperature to work; after that, the refrigerator is where the jar should live.

梅干菜 is the driest end of the Hakka mustard-green family. Taiwan's 農業部 describes it as 福菜 that has been sun-dried until completely dry and then rolled into balls, and says the reason it keeps longer is precisely that there is no water left in it. An airtight jar in a cool dark cupboard; never a damp hand or a wet spoon in the jar. Bloom of salt crystals on the surface is normal.
For best aroma once the bag is opened. It stays safe far longer if it stays genuinely dry, but the smoky-sweet smell that is the whole point of the ingredient fades.

Wetter members of the family behave differently and should be cold. 福菜 is packed damp in an inverted jar and is still a wet pickle; 酸菜 is a straight brine ferment that 農業部 describes as ready after about a week and which should be kept in its liquid in the fridge once opened. No agency publishes cold-storage times for either, so none are given here.

A fresh soft pretzel is a same-morning food and it deteriorates faster than any other bread in this file. Two things work against it at once: the lye bath leaves a thin, deeply browned skin that goes leathery as soon as the crumb's moisture migrates outward, and the coarse salt on top is hygroscopic — it pulls water from the air and dissolves into wet patches. Leave it unwrapped and eat it. Wrapping makes it soggy; not wrapping makes it dry.
No. Cold accelerates staling in a lean dough and this is about as lean as they come.

The one thing that works. Freeze them the hour they cool, bagged, and reheat from frozen at 180 °C for 6 to 8 minutes; brush with a little water and re-salt if the salt has dissolved. Commercially frozen pretzels are packed to keep far longer — FoodKeeper gives 9 months for those, and once cooked they keep 3 to 4 days refrigerated.
The shell dries and browns quickly at room temperature even though the flesh inside is still good.
Seal in a bag to hold humidity — the loss of shell colour is water loss, not spoilage.

NMSU gives cooked fish and shellfish 3 to 4 days at or below 40 °F (4 °C). Cool it fast — pull the tentacles out of the hot cooking water, spread them on a tray, and refrigerate within 2 hours; a whole octopus left to cool in its pot stays warm for hours. Keeping it under a little of its own cooking liquor stops it drying, but does not extend the window.

Freeze the cooked tentacles whole rather than sliced, with a splash of the cooking liquor. Freezing raw octopus before cooking is the old trick for tenderness — the ice crystals break down the muscle — and it works, so buying it frozen is no loss.
Refrigeration not necessary for unsalted pumpkin seeds.

Keep it at or below 40 °F (4 °C) — the FDA's explicit instruction for this cheese — sealed, and away from anything ready-to-eat. FDA is blunter still about leftovers: 'Do not keep leftover queso fresco-type cheeses after they have been opened to minimize the risk of Listeria growth.' Discard it if it has sat between 40 °F and 140 °F for more than 2 hours.

Freezing works for cooking only. The curd turns grainy and weeps on thawing, so use frozen queso fresco crumbled into a filling or melted into a sauce, never sliced onto a plate. Freezing does not kill Listeria — it only stops it multiplying.

Unopened and vacuum-packed it holds for weeks at or below 40 °F (4 °C). Once the ball is broken into, wrap the remainder tightly and use it within about a week — every pulled strand is a new surface. It should squeak and pull; a slick, sour or ammoniacal surface means it is done.
Freeze it as an unbroken ball or in wound skeins, double-wrapped. It thaws crumbly and loses some of the pull, so freeze it for quesadillas and tlayudas rather than for eating in strands.
Quince is rock hard and keeps well in a cool room; a bowl of them will perfume a kitchen. Store away from other fruit, which picks up the scent.
Wrap loosely; the skin bruises brown where it knocks. Ohio State gives apples 1 to 3 weeks in the fridge, and quince, being denser and harder, holds considerably longer.
Freeze peeled, cored and poached — raw quince flesh browns and stays woody.

Unopened, to the date on the vacuum pack, at 0–5 °C. Raclette is a washed-rind cheese, which means the rind was deliberately kept damp and bacterially alive during ripening — it is moister and less acidic than a cheddar and it does not keep like one. The smell is the rind doing its job; ammonia is not.

Ohio State gives opened hard cheese 3 to 4 weeks, which is the right order of magnitude for a firm raclette wedge, though a very ripe or very moist one will be closer to two. Wrap it in waxed or greaseproof paper inside a loose box, not in clingfilm against the cut face — the cheese needs to breathe or the rind sweats and slimes.
